objectivesPlain: By the end, you can explain why a machine trained on examples from one group can make more mistakes for people outside that group.
You can work out a percentage for each group, and show how one overall number can hide a big gap.
You can suggest a fair fix: add the missing examples and test each group separately, instead of adding more of the same.
before: Click through the lesson once in classroom mode (about 10 minutes).
On the board, draw two ways to write 1 (a plain line; a line with a long sloping flag at the top) and two ways to write 7 (plain; with a line across the middle).
Draw a tally table on the board with columns: Writer, Machine says, Right or wrong.

timing.teacherDoes: Project the post office story. Ask: the machine is 97% accurate, so why do some letters still go to the wrong town?
timing.studentsDo: Two or three students give a guess aloud.

timing.teacherDoes: Read the three choices. Count hands for each and write the numbers on the board.
Read each card; the class calls out its label; press Train the machine. Before each new writer's result, the class guesses.
timing.studentsDo: Call out labels; vote on each of the 4 writers; fill the tally table.

timing.teacherDoes: Show the check. Work 1 out of 2 = 50 out of 100 on the board. Compare with 3 of 4 = 75% overall.
timing.studentsDo: Vote on 50%, 75% or 12%; one student explains.

timing.teacherDoes: Run the second machine with 8 cards from many writers. Ask: what changed, the machine or the data?
timing.studentsDo: Label the cards aloud; compare the new results with the tally table.

timing.teacherDoes: Reveal sample and bias. Step through the cook and rainy-week comparisons, stopping at 'where it breaks'.
timing.studentsDo: Pairs say one way the cook is like the machine and one way it is not.

timing.teacherDoes: Run the 97%-but-0% check, then the break-it writers and the 'add 1,000 more school cards' check.
timing.studentsDo: Vote on each; predict whether each new writer fools the machine.

timing.teacherDoes: Run the responsibility vote. Take two views that disagree. Read the takeaway card aloud.
timing.studentsDo: Vote; one or two explain their choice; write one sentence in their notebook.

ifShortOfTime: Skip the rainy-week comparison and the break-it writers. Keep the two machines, the 50% check and the responsibility vote.

misconceptions.studentsSay: The machine was trained, so it should work for everybody.
misconceptions.goodResponse: It works for writing like its examples. Writing unlike any example gets the label of the nearest examples, which can be wrong.

misconceptions.studentsSay: The people with the flag 1 write badly.
misconceptions.goodResponse: Their 1 is a correct, common way to write it. The gap was in the data, not in their writing.
97% is for everyone together. Check each group: flag writers could be at 0%.

misconceptions.studentsSay: Add more data and it will be fixed.
misconceptions.goodResponse: More of the same school's cards still has no flag 1s. Add the missing kind.

misconceptions.studentsSay: The machine decided to be unfair.
misconceptions.goodResponse: It has no intentions. It copies labels from the closest examples. People choose the data.

discussionPrompts: Who should be responsible when data leaves people out: the collectors, the company, the users, or everyone?
Where else in life could one overall number hide a group that is doing badly?
noDeviceAlternative: Use the board drawings as the cards. Write the 6 school cards (3 plain 1s, 3 plain 7s) as a 'dataset'. For each new writer, ask: which cards does it look most like? Take the label most of those 3 cards share. Students vote by hands, then record right or wrong in the tally table. Repeat with 8 cards that include flag 1s and crossed 7s. Students compute percentages in notebooks and write their responsibility sentence.
ifYouDontKnow: Say: 'Good question. I am not sure. Let us write it on the board and look it up together.' The main idea is enough: machines copy patterns from the examples they get, and people choose those examples.
parentNote: Today your child trained a simple computer program on handwriting examples from one school. It read other writing styles badly, until they added the missing examples. Ask them: who should fix it when a machine is unfair to some people?
